chapters.title: Marketing: Core Concepts, Philosophies and the Marketing Mix
chapters.scope: What marketing is, how the idea of it has changed, and the mixes (4Ps, 4Cs, 4As) used to plan it.

blocks.title: What marketing is
blocks.html:
The American Marketing Association (definition approved 2017) defines marketing as “the activity, set of institutions, and processes for creating, communicating, delivering, and exchanging offerings that have value for customers, clients, partners, and society at large”. Philip Kotler calls it the social and managerial process by which individuals and groups obtain what they need and want through creating and exchanging products and value with others. Kotler and Keller's shortest definition is “meeting needs profitably”.

Marketing is not simply the art of selling, as it is sometimes described. Peter Drucker argued the opposite: the aim of marketing is to know and understand the customer so well that the product fits and sells itself, which makes selling superfluous.

ConceptMeaningExample
NeedA state of felt deprivation: basic requirements such as food, safety and belongingHunger
WantThe form a need takes, shaped by culture and individual personalityA dosa, or a burger
DemandA want backed by the ability and willingness to payBuying a ₹120 dosa at a restaurant

Needs may be physical (food, clothing, shelter), social (belonging, affection, recognition) or individual (knowledge, self-expression). Example: the need is to quench thirst, the want is water, and the demand is a particular brand of bottled water the buyer can pay for.

AspectExchangeTransaction
MeaningThe process of obtaining a desired product from someone by offering something of value in returnA trade of values between two parties, the unit of exchange
InvolvesAt least two parties, each with something the other values, free to accept or rejectAt least two things of value, agreed conditions, a time and a place
ExampleBarterA purchase, or a banking transaction

Marketing works through exchange, which takes place because the buyer expects satisfaction from the product's utility, the value that makes it able to satisfy a want.

UtilityValue added by…
FormTurning materials into a usable product; created mainly by production, guided by marketing research
PlaceMaking the product available where buyers want it
TimeMaking it available when they want it
PossessionTransferring ownership, helped by credit and easy payment
InformationTelling buyers that the product exists and what it does
EntityExamples
GoodsPackaged foods, cars, phones
ServicesAirlines, banking, repairs; many offers, such as a restaurant meal, mix goods and services
EventsTrade shows, sporting events, festivals
ExperiencesTheme parks, river rafting, bungee jumping
PersonsArtists, performers, sportspeople, politicians
PlacesCities, states and countries: ‘Incredible India’, Kerala's ‘God's Own Country’
PropertiesReal estate, financial property such as shares
OrganisationsCompanies, universities, the armed forces recruiting
InformationEncyclopaedias, data, maps
IdeasSocial causes and new practices, such as digital payments

Need, want plus buying power, demand.

blocks.title: States of demand
blocks.html:
Marketers manage demand, not just respond to it. Philip Kotler (1973) described eight states of demand, each calling for a different marketing task.

StateSituationMarketing task
Negative demandMuch of the market dislikes the product and may even pay to avoid it, as with vaccinations or dental workConversional marketing: find out why, and change attitudes through redesign, lower prices or promotion
No demandBuyers are unaware of the product or uninterested in itStimulational marketing: connect the product's benefits to people's needs
Latent demandA strong need exists that no existing product satisfies, as for a truly affordable electric carDevelopmental marketing: measure the potential market and develop the product
Declining demandBuyers are buying less, or moving to newer productsRemarketing: reverse the decline with new markets, features or communication
Irregular demandPurchases vary by season, day or hour, as with raincoats or mosquito repellentSynchromarketing: smooth demand with flexible pricing and promotion
Full demandBuyers are buying all the products put on the marketMaintenance marketing: keep quality up and watch satisfaction
Overfull demandMore buyers want the product than can be satisfied, as with train tickets in the holiday seasonDemarketing: reduce demand temporarily, for example by raising prices or cutting promotion
Unwholesome demandThe product has undesirable social consequences, as with tobaccoCountermarketing: persuade people to give it up, through warnings, high prices or reduced availability

Negative, none, latent, declining, irregular, full, overfull, unwholesome.

blocks.title: How marketing philosophies evolved
blocks.html:
ConceptBeliefFocus
ProductionConsumers prefer products that are widely available and cheapEfficient production and wide distribution
ProductConsumers prefer the best quality, performance and featuresContinuous product improvement; risks ‘marketing myopia’
SellingConsumers will not buy enough unless persuadedAggressive selling and promotion of what the firm makes
MarketingThe key is to know the target market's needs and satisfy them better than competitorsCustomer needs: ‘sense and respond’ rather than ‘make and sell’
Societal marketingThe firm should also serve consumers' and society's long-term well-beingCompany profit, consumer wants and society's interests together
Holistic marketingEverything matters; the business is one connected systemBreadth and interdependence of all marketing activity

Marketing myopia (Theodore Levitt, 1960) is defining a business by its product rather than by the need it meets, as railways did by seeing themselves in the railroad business rather than in transport. Levitt also drew the contrast between selling, which focuses on the seller's need to turn products into cash, and marketing, which focuses on the buyer's needs. Selling works inside-out, from the factory; marketing works outside-in, from the market.

AspectSellingMarketing
EmphasisThe productCustomers' needs and wants
SequenceMake the product first, then work out how to sell itFind out what customers want, then design the product to satisfy it
ProfitFrom sales volumeFrom customer satisfaction and keeping customers over the long run
ViewpointThe seller's needsThe buyer's needs

Holistic marketing (Kotler and Keller) has four components: relationship marketing (lasting ties with customers, employees and partners), integrated marketing (all activities combined to create, communicate and deliver value), internal marketing (hiring, training and motivating staff to serve customers well, from top management down) and performance marketing (financial returns and the wider ethical, social and environmental effects). Earlier editions named the fourth socially responsible marketing, a label many study notes still use.

Production, product, selling, marketing, societal, holistic.

blocks.title: The marketing mix: 4Ps, 4Cs and 4As
blocks.html:
The marketing mix is the set of controllable tools a firm blends to get the response it wants from its target market. Neil Borden popularised the term (his 1964 article describes using it from 1949); E. Jerome McCarthy (1960) grouped the tools into the 4Ps. Robert Lauterborn (1990) restated them from the customer's side as the 4Cs, and Jagdish Sheth and Rajendra Sisodia offered the 4As, also from the buyer's viewpoint.

4Ps (seller)4Cs (Lauterborn)4As (Sheth and Sisodia)
ProductCustomer solution (value)Acceptability: does it meet the customer's functional and psychological needs?
PriceCustomer costAffordability: are customers able and willing to pay?
PlaceConvenienceAccessibility: can customers readily get it?
PromotionCommunicationAwareness: do customers know about it and what it does?

Services add three more Ps (people, process and physical evidence), covered in the services chapter.

Product, price, place, promotion, seen from the buyer's side.

blocks.title: Forces reshaping marketing
blocks.html:
Kotler and Keller name the major societal forces that keep changing what marketers must do. Strategies that are not revised as these forces change soon lose their relevance.

ForceWhat it means
Network information technologyThe digital revolution allows more accurate production, more targeted communication and more relevant pricing
GlobalisationCheaper transport and communication let firms sell in, and consumers buy from, almost any country
Deregulation and privatisationOpening industries to competition, and turning public companies over to private ownership
Heightened competitionDomestic and foreign brands compete hard, raising marketing costs and shrinking margins
Industry convergenceIndustry boundaries blur, as computing and consumer electronics have merged
Retail transformationStores compete with TV shopping and e-commerce, and respond by selling an experience
DisintermediationOnline sellers bypass traditional channels; traditional firms respond with re-intermediation, becoming ‘brick-and-click’ rather than ‘pure-click’
Consumer buying power, information and participationBuyers compare prices and features anywhere, at any time, find information in depth, and influence peers and public opinion
Consumer resistanceSeeing fewer real differences between products, buyers are less loyal, more price- and quality-sensitive, and less tolerant of unwanted marketing

New capabilities. The same forces give marketers new tools: the internet as an information and sales channel with worldwide reach; richer data about markets and individual customers; social media and brand communities to amplify messages and buzz; permission-based ads, coupons and samples; mobile, location-based marketing near the point of sale; mass customisation of products; online recruiting, training and internal communication; and cost savings from comparing suppliers online and running reverse auctions.

Technology, globalisation and empowered buyers keep changing the task.

text: The Kuṟaḷ says the proper trade of traders is to guard the interests of others as their own. The marketing concept rests on the same reversal of view, from what the seller wants to sell to what the buyer needs.
pairings.quote: “For those who trade, true trade is to care for others' goods and interests as their own.” வாணிகம் செய்வார்க்கு வாணிகம் பேணிப் பிறவும் தமபோல் செயின். Tirukkuṟaḷ 120

chapters.title: Segmentation, Targeting and Positioning
chapters.scope: How a firm divides a market, chooses whom to serve, and earns a distinct place in their minds.

blocks.title: Market segmentation
blocks.html:
STP, segmentation, targeting and positioning, is the sequence at the heart of marketing strategy. Market segmentation divides a market into distinct groups of buyers with similar needs, characteristics or behaviour, who might want different products or marketing.

Segments can be defined by descriptive characteristics (geographic, demographic, psychographic), checking whether the groups differ in needs or responses; or by behavioural responses (benefits sought, usage occasions, brands), checking whether each response group has a distinct profile. Do car buyers who want quality rather than a low price differ in age, income or lifestyle?

LevelApproachWhat it doesExample
MacroMass (undifferentiated) marketingMass production, distribution and promotion of one product for all buyers: ‘one size fits all’One advertisement for milk aimed at every household
MicroSegment marketingDifferent offers for large groups with similar wants, buying power and habitsTerm insurance plans for young earners
MicroNiche marketingA narrower group with distinct needs, often willing to pay a premiumLuxury watches and sports cars
MicroLocal marketingProgrammes tailored to the needs of local customers: cities, neighbourhoods, storesA neighbourhood bakery or florist
MicroIndividual marketingThe ultimate level: customised or one-to-one marketingA custom-made wedding dress; made-to-order car interiors
BasisVariables
GeographicCountry, region, state, city size, urban or rural, climate
DemographicAge, gender, income, education, occupation, family size and life cycle, religion
PsychographicLifestyle, personality, values and interests; lifestyle is often measured by activities, interests and opinions (the AIO approach of William Wells and Douglas Tigert, 1971)
BehaviouralOccasions (weddings, birthdays), benefits sought (quality, service, economy), user status (non-user, ex-user, first-time user), usage rate (light, heavy), loyalty status (none, medium, strong), readiness stage (unaware, aware, intending to buy), attitude to the product

Demographic variables are popular because they are linked to needs and easy to measure; even a segment described by personality has to be linked back to demographics to estimate its size and choose media to reach it. Psychographics adds psychology: people with the same demographics can have very different lifestyles, personalities and values.

Business markets are segmented by demographic or firmographic variables (industry, company size, location), operating variables (technology used, user status, customer capabilities), purchasing approaches (purchasing policies, buying criteria, how buying is organised), situational factors (urgency, order size) and the personal characteristics of the buyers. This nested approach is Thomas Bonoma and Benson Shapiro's (1983).

Useful segments are measurable, substantial (large and profitable enough), accessible, differentiable (they respond differently) and actionable (the firm can design programmes for them).

Geographic, demographic, psychographic, behavioural.

blocks.title: Targeting
blocks.html:
Targeting is choosing which segments to serve. Each segment is evaluated on its size and growth, its structural attractiveness (competition, substitutes, buyer and supplier power), and its fit with the firm's objectives and resources.

PatternWhat the firm serves
Single-segment concentrationOne segment with one product
Selective specialisationSeveral unrelated segments, each attractive on its own
Product specialisationOne product sold to several segments
Market specialisationMany needs of one particular customer group, with several products
Full market coverageAll customer groups with all the products they need, by undifferentiated or differentiated marketing

Examples. A luxury watchmaker concentrates on one high-end segment. A maker of nuts and bolts that sells different types to car makers, electrical-equipment makers and builders practises product specialisation. A firm selling an assortment of products only to ice-cream makers practises market specialisation. Only very large firms, such as Hindustan Unilever, Nestlé or Coca-Cola in non-alcoholic drinks, can attempt full market coverage.

These five patterns follow Derek Abell (1980) and are used by Kotler and Keller. Seen as strategies, targeting runs from undifferentiated (mass) marketing, through differentiated (segmented) and concentrated (niche) marketing, to micromarketing.

Evaluate the segments, then choose a pattern of coverage.

blocks.title: Positioning
blocks.html:
Positioning is designing the firm's offering and image to occupy a distinct, valued place in the minds of the target market. Al Ries and Jack Trout made the idea famous (Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind, 1981): positioning is not what you do to a product but what you do to the prospect's mind.

TypeMeaningRole
Points of difference (PODs)Attributes or benefits that customers strongly associate with the brand, rate positively, and believe they could not find to the same extent in a competitorGive customers a reason to choose the brand
Points of parity (POPs)Associations that are not unique but are needed for the brand to be credible in its category, or that neutralise a competitor's points of differenceRemove reasons not to choose it

This pairing is Kevin Lane Keller's. A value proposition is the full set of benefits on which the brand is positioned, often summed up as more for more, more for the same, the same for less, less for much less, or more for less.

Brands can be positioned on attributes, benefits, use or application, user, competitor, product class, or price and quality.

Positioning lives in the customer's mind, not in the product.

blocks.title: Differentiation and the brand bull's-eye
blocks.html:
A firm positions its offer by differentiating it from competitors'. Kotler and Keller name five main bases.

BasisVariablesExample
ProductForm, features, performance, conformance, durability, reliability, repairability, style, designPhones that compete on design and performance
ServicesOrdering ease, delivery, installation, customer training, customer consulting, maintenance and repair, returnsPizza chains competing on delivery time; air-conditioner makers on installation
PersonnelCompetence, courtesy, credibility, reliability, responsiveness, communicationService firms depend heavily on their people
ChannelCoverage, expertise, performanceE-commerce and other delivery-dependent businesses
ImageSymbols (such as McDonald's golden arches), atmosphere, media, events and sponsorshipsBrands built on a recognisable identity

Is it a real point of difference? Keller's three tests: it must be desirable to consumers (personally relevant), deliverable by the company (it has the resources and commitment to create and keep the association profitably), and differentiating from competitors (seen as distinctive and superior).

KindMeaningExample
Category POPsWhat consumers see as essential for a credible offer in the category: necessary but not sufficient for choice; they change with technology, law and trendsA travel agency must book flights and hotels, advise on packages and offer payment options
Competitive POPsAssociations designed to negate a competitor's points of difference, or a weakness created by the brand's own points of differenceA low-priced brand reassuring buyers on quality

The brand-positioning bull's-eye (Kotler and Keller) communicates the positioning to everyone in the organisation. At its centre are the brand mantra (the brand's essence in a few words) and the key points of parity and difference; around them are the reasons to believe, facts that support those points; the outer ring holds the brand's values, personality or character and its executional properties and visual identity. Boxes beside it record the inputs (the target consumer and a key insight; the competitive need and rival brands) and the output: the ideal consumer takeaway.

Differentiate on product, services, people, channel or image; test it as desirable, deliverable, differentiating.

text: Segmentation starts from the fact that different audiences need different offers. The Kuṟaḷ asks speakers who are pure and know the range of words to study the assembly before they speak. It is about addressing a gathering, not about dividing a market.
pairings.quote: “Those of pure mind who know the range of words should study the assembly and then speak.” அவையறிந்து ஆராய்ந்து சொல்லுக சொல்லின் தொகையறிந்த தூய்மை யவர். Tirukkuṟaḷ 711

chapters.title: Product Decisions: Levels, New Products and the Life Cycle
chapters.scope: What a product is to a buyer, how new products are developed and adopted, and how strategy changes as a product ages.

blocks.title: Product levels and classification
blocks.html:
A product is anything offered to a market to satisfy a want or need: physical goods, services, experiences, events, places, ideas and more. Buyers see it at several levels, each adding customer value.

LevelMeaningExample: a smartphone
Core product (core customer value)The basic benefit or problem-solving service the buyer is really seekingStaying connected
Actual productThe tangible offer: features, quality, design, brand name and packagingThe phone itself, its brand and box
Augmented productExtra services and benefits: delivery, installation, warranty, after-sales service, supportWarranty, repair network, cloud backup

Kotler and Keller describe five levels in a customer-value hierarchy: core benefit, basic product, expected product, augmented product, and potential product (all the changes it might undergo in future). Competition increasingly takes place at the augmented level. Some texts call the actual product the formal product.

TypeBuying behaviourExamples
ConvenienceBought often, quickly, with little comparisonSoap, newspapers, snacks
ShoppingCompared on quality, price and style before buyingFurniture, clothing, appliances
SpecialtyUnique features or brand; buyers make a special effortLuxury watches, designer clothes
UnsoughtNot known of, or not normally thought of buyingLife insurance, blood donation

Core benefit, actual product, augmented product.

blocks.title: Product mix and product lines
blocks.html:
A product item is a specific version of a product: one model, brand or size. A product line is a group of closely related products made or sold by the same firm. The product mix (product assortment) is the complete set of all product lines and items a company offers for sale.

DimensionMeaningExample
WidthThe number of different product linesA consumer-goods firm with lines in personal wash, laundry, skin care, hair care, oral care, deodorants, tea and coffee has a width of eight
LengthThe total number of items across all its linesThose eight lines might hold 23 brands in all
DepthThe number of variants of each product in a line, by size, flavour, formulation and so onA toothpaste offered in three formulations and three sizes has a depth of 3 × 3 = 9
ConsistencyHow closely the lines are related in use, production, distribution or other waysLines all sold through grocery stores are consistent in distribution

These four dimensions give the firm four ways to grow: add lines (width), lengthen lines, add variants (depth), or make the mix more or less consistent.

Width: lines. Length: items. Depth: variants. Consistency: relatedness.

blocks.title: New product development and adoption
blocks.html:
Kotler and Armstrong describe new product development (NPD) in eight steps. Many study notes give seven, leaving out marketing strategy development.

StepWhat happens
1 Idea generationSystematic search for ideas from customers, employees, competitors, suppliers and R&D
2 Idea screeningDropping poor ideas early, since costs rise at each later step
3 Concept development and testingTurning the idea into a detailed concept and testing it with target customers
4 Marketing strategy developmentPlanning the target market, positioning, price, distribution and marketing budget
5 Business analysisEstimating sales, costs and profits to see if they meet the firm's objectives
6 Product developmentBuilding a working prototype and testing it
7 Test marketingTrying the product and its marketing in realistic market settings
8 CommercialisationFull launch: deciding when, where, to whom and how

Adoption. Everett Rogers (Diffusion of Innovations, 1962) grouped adopters by how early they take up an innovation: innovators (2.5 per cent), early adopters (13.5), early majority (34), late majority (34) and laggards (16).

Generate, screen, test the concept, plan the strategy, analyse, develop, test-market, launch.

blocks.title: The product life cycle
blocks.html:
The product life cycle (PLC) traces a product's sales and profits over its life. Each stage calls for a different strategy (Theodore Levitt, “Exploit the Product Life Cycle”, 1965, is a classic account).

AspectIntroductionGrowthMaturityDecline
SalesLowRising fastPeakFalling
ProfitsNegative or lowRisingHighDeclining
CustomersInnovatorsEarly adoptersMiddle majorityLaggards
CompetitorsFewGrowingStable, then decliningDeclining
Marketing objectiveCreate awareness and trialMaximise market shareMaximise profit while defending shareCut spending and milk the brand
ProductBasic productExtensions, service, warrantyDiversify brands and modelsPhase out weak items
PriceCost-plus, or skimmingPrice to penetrateMatch or beat competitorsCut price
DistributionSelectiveIntensiveMore intensiveSelective: drop unprofitable outlets
PromotionBuild awareness among early adopters and dealersBuild awareness and interest in the mass marketStress brand differences and benefitsReduce to the minimum needed to keep loyal customers

Not every product follows the smooth curve. Styles come and go in cycles, fashions rise slowly and decline slowly, and fads rise and collapse quickly.

Introduce, grow, mature, decline: change the mix at each stage.

pairings.modern: The rise and fall of demand
text: The PLC describes sales that gather, peak and fall away. The Kuṟaḷ compares great wealth to a theatre crowd: it gathers like the audience for a show, and leaves as the crowd disperses when the show ends. The couplet is about the impermanence of riches, not about products.
pairings.quote: “Great wealth gathers like the crowd at a play, and goes as that crowd disperses.” கூத்தாட்டு அவைக்குழாத் தற்றே பெருஞ்செல்வம் போக்கும் அதுவிளிந் தற்று. Tirukkuṟaḷ 332

chapters.title: Brand Management: Equity, Strategy and Loyalty
chapters.scope: What a brand is worth, the decisions that build it, how brands are extended, and how loyal their buyers become.

blocks.title: Brands and brand equity
blocks.html:
A brand, in the AMA's definition, is a name, term, sign, symbol or design, or a combination of them, intended to identify the goods or services of one seller and to differentiate them from competitors. A brand strategy is the long-term plan to build, position and sustain the brand; unlike a campaign, it is long-term and emotion-driven, aiming at growth, customer loyalty and a strong market position.

What brands do. For consumers, a brand identifies the maker and lets buyers hold it responsible; the same product can be judged differently depending on how it is branded; and brands simplify decisions and reduce risk. For firms, brands simplify handling and record-keeping, give legal protection (trademarks for names, patents for processes, copyright and designs for packaging), signal quality so satisfied buyers can choose again, and create loyalty that makes demand predictable and builds barriers to entry. Kotler and Keller note that loyalty can let a brand charge 20 to 25 per cent more than competitors. Rivals can copy processes and designs, but not the impressions years of experience and marketing leave in buyers' minds.

AspectBrand equityBrand value
MeaningThe added value a brand gives a product in customers' mindsThe brand's financial worth
NatureTrust, preference and loyaltyA monetary asset
Shows inCustomers paying a premium, as for AppleValuations in mergers and acquisitions

Kevin Lane Keller defines customer-based brand equity as the differential effect that brand knowledge has on consumer response to the marketing of that brand. Brand equity is reflected in the perceptions, preferences and behaviour related to all aspects of the brand's marketing. If customers respond no differently to a branded product than to an unbranded one, the product is essentially a commodity, and competition will probably be based on price.

Keller's definition has three ingredients: brand equity arises from differences in consumer response; those differences come from consumers' brand knowledge, all the thoughts, feelings, images, experiences and beliefs linked to the brand, which must be strong, favourable and unique, as Toyota's link to reliability is; and equity shows in perceptions, preferences and behaviour across all of the brand's marketing. Equity is positive when consumers react more favourably to the marketing once they know the brand, and negative when they react less favourably. The brand promise is the marketer's vision of what the brand must be and do for consumers.

ModelComponents
David Aaker (1991)Brand loyalty, brand awareness, perceived quality, brand associations, and other proprietary assets such as patents
Keller's customer-based brand equity pyramidSalience (identity), then performance and imagery (meaning), then judgements and feelings (response), and at the top resonance (relationship)

Equity lives in customers' minds; value is what the brand is worth in money.

blocks.title: Brand equity models
blocks.html:
Kotler and Keller describe several models of brand equity. They share principles but stress different things.

PillarMeasures
Energised differentiationHow far the brand is seen as different from others, and its momentum and leadership
RelevanceHow appropriate and broad the brand's appeal is
EsteemHow well the brand is regarded and respected: perceived quality and loyalty
KnowledgeHow aware and familiar consumers are with the brand

Differentiation and relevance together give brand strength, a leading indicator of future growth; esteem and knowledge together give brand stature, a report card on past performance. Plotting strength against stature gives a power grid of the brand's stage of development: new brands show more differentiation and energy than relevance, with low esteem and knowledge; leadership brands are high on all four; declining brands show high knowledge but lower esteem and lower still relevance and differentiation.

LevelThe consumer…
PresenceIs actively familiar with the brand, through trial, salience or knowledge of its promise
RelevanceFinds it relevant to their needs, in the right price range or in the consideration set
PerformanceBelieves it performs acceptably and puts it on the short-list
AdvantageBelieves it has an emotional or rational advantage over others in the category
BondingIs attached to it, rationally and emotionally, to the exclusion of most other brands

Bonded consumers build stronger relationships with the brand and spend more on it; since most consumers sit at the lower levels, the marketer's task is to move them up.

Keller's brand resonance model sees brand building as four ascending steps, each answering a consumer's question: identity (who are you?), meaning (what are you?), response (what about you: what do I think and feel?) and relationships (what about you and me?). They rest on six building blocks: salience at the base; performance and imagery; judgements and feelings; and resonance at the top, the intensity of the customer's bond with the brand, seen in brands such as Harley-Davidson and Apple. The left side of the pyramid is the rational route and the right side the emotional route; MasterCard combined both, stressing worldwide acceptance and, in its ‘Priceless’ campaign, the things money can't buy.

Aaker's model (1991) defines brand equity as a set of assets and liabilities linked to a brand that add to or subtract from the value of a product, under five heads: brand loyalty, brand awareness, perceived quality, brand associations, and other proprietary assets such as patents and trademarks.

BAV's four pillars, BrandZ's pyramid, Keller's resonance, Aaker's five assets.

blocks.title: Major brand strategy decisions
blocks.html:
DecisionOptions
Brand positioningOn product attributes, on benefits, or, the strongest, on beliefs and values that carry emotional weight
Brand name selectionA good name suggests the benefits, is easy to say and remember, distinctive, extendable, translatable, legally protectable, and free of bad meanings in other languages
Brand sponsorshipManufacturer's (national) brand, private (store) brand, licensed brand, or co-branding
Brand developmentLine extensions, brand extensions, multibrands or new brands
StrategyHow it works
Individual namesA separate name for each product; one failure does not harm the company name
Blanket family nameOne name for all products; new products gain acceptance quickly
Separate family namesA different family name for each category
Corporate name with individual namesThe company name legitimises the product, the individual name gives it its own identity
TermMeaning
Brand lineAll products sold under one brand
Brand mix (assortment)All the brand lines a seller offers
Branded variantsVersions of a brand made for particular retailers or channels, as Maruti Suzuki sells different models through its Arena and Nexa showrooms
Licensed productA product carrying a brand that its owner has licensed to another manufacturer

A firm's branding strategy, often called its brand architecture, sets the number and nature of the brand elements its products share or keep distinct. To brand a new product, a firm can develop new brand elements, apply some of its existing ones, or combine new and existing elements.

Positioning on attributes is the least effective level, since attributes are easy to copy; benefits associate the name with something desirable; beliefs and values tap emotions. Licensing leases a brand name for use in a defined way, territory and period.

Position, name, sponsor, develop.

blocks.title: Brand portfolios
blocks.html:
A brand portfolio is the set of all brands and brand lines a firm offers in a particular category or market segment. A brand can be stretched only so far, and not every segment the firm wants will view one brand equally well, so firms often need several brands.

Why have several brands in one category? To gain more shelf space and retailer dependence, to keep variety-seeking consumers who would otherwise switch, to create internal competition, and to gain economies of scale in advertising, selling, merchandising and distribution.

RoleWhat it doesExample
Flanker (fighter)Positioned against competitors' brands so that the more important, more profitable flagship can keep its desired positionA cheaper second brand launched against a price-cutting rival
Cash cowKept despite falling sales because it stays profitable with almost no marketing support; the firm ‘milks’ its reservoir of equityAn older car model kept on sale because withdrawing it might not move buyers to the firm's other models
Low-end entry levelA relatively low-priced ‘traffic builder’ that draws customers into the brand franchise so they can later be traded upEntry models of a luxury carmaker
High-end prestigeA relatively high-priced brand that adds prestige and credibility to the whole portfolioA flagship superbike that draws visitors to the showroom and lifts the image of the maker's other motorcycles

Flankers, cash cows, entry brands, prestige brands.

blocks.title: Brand extensions
blocks.html:
A brand extension uses an established (parent) brand to launch a new product. A parent brand that supports several extensions is a family or master brand. A sub-brand combines a new name with an existing one, as in Cadbury Dairy Milk Silk.

TypeWhat changesExample
Line extensionA new item in the same category under the same brand: new flavours, forms, sizes or packagingA new noodle variety under a noodle brand
Category extensionThe brand enters a different product categoryA noodle brand launching ketchup

Kotler and Armstrong's four brand development choices form a grid: line extensions (existing brand, existing category), brand extensions (existing brand, new category), multibrands (new brands in an existing category, to capture different segments) and new brands (new brand, new category). A flanker or fighter brand is a lower-priced brand launched to protect the flagship from competitors.

AdvantagesLimitations
Lower perceived risk for buyers; quicker acceptanceBrand dilution: the brand's meaning blurs
Lower marketing and launch costsConsumer confusion
Can strengthen the parent brandRetailer resistance to more variants
Wider market coverageCannibalisation of the parent's sales; a failure can hurt the parent; a missed chance to build a new brand

Benefits in more detail. Extensions improve the odds of new-product success: consumers form expectations from what they know of the parent, retailers are readier to stock the product, the launch campaign need only introduce the product rather than the brand too, and the firm saves the cost of a new name and gains packaging and labelling efficiencies. They can also feed back positively, clarifying the brand's meaning, renewing interest in it, widening its coverage and opening the way to further extensions.

Risks in more detail. The brand may become less strongly identified with any one product; a brand known for Ayurvedic products that moves into jeans, for example, risks its specific meaning. Inappropriate extensions can confuse or frustrate consumers and make them question the brand's integrity. The worst case, which is rare, is an extension that fails and harms the parent. ‘Marketing failures’, where too few people try the product, do much less damage than ‘product failures’, where it fails to live up to its promise, and even product failures dilute equity mainly when the extension closely resembles the parent. Sales of an extension may simply be cannibalised from the parent, though that may be pre-emptive cannibalisation if buyers would otherwise have switched to a competitor.

Co-branding puts two established brands on one product, so each brand's strength supports the other.

Extend the line, extend the brand, add brands, or start anew.

blocks.title: Brand loyalty
blocks.html:
Brand loyalty is the extent of a customer's faithfulness to a brand, shown in repeat purchases and in positive behaviour such as word-of-mouth advocacy, whatever marketing pressure competing brands apply. David Aaker (1991) arranged its levels in a pyramid, from no loyalty at the base to full commitment at the top. Study notes often give the levels in a muddled order; the version below follows Aaker.

LevelBuyer
1 SwitchersPrice-sensitive and indifferent; no loyalty to any brand
2 Habitual buyersSatisfied or at least not dissatisfied; no reason to change
3 Satisfied buyers with switching costsWould lose time, money or risk by changing
4 Brand likersLike the brand and regard it as a friend
5 Committed buyersProud to use the brand and recommend it

Switchers, habitual, switching costs, likers, committed.

text: Brand equity is reputation that has become an asset. The Kuṟaḷ says that to give and to live with renown is the only real gain of life. It speaks of a person's good name earned through generosity, not of a commercial brand.
pairings.quote: “To give, and to live with renown: there is no other gain for a life.” ஈதல் இசைபட வாழ்தல் அதுவல்லது ஊதியம் இல்லை உயிர்க்கு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 231

text: Co-branding lends one brand the standing of another. The Kuṟaḷ says that goodness of mind brings prosperity, and good company brings every kind of renown. It is about a person's associates, not about brand partnerships.
pairings.quote: “Goodness of mind brings prosperity to people; goodness of company brings all renown.” மனநலம் மன்னுயிர்க் காக்கம் இனநலம் எல்லாப் புகழும் தரும். Tirukkuṟaḷ 457

text: A weak extension is seen at once because the parent is so well known. The Kuṟaḷ says a fault in those of noble family stands out like the spot on the moon high in the sky. Its subject is conduct and lineage, not brands.
pairings.quote: “A fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon high in the sky.” குடிப்பிறந்தார் கண்விளங்கும் குற்றம் விசும்பின் மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து. Tirukkuṟaḷ 957

text: At the top of Aaker's pyramid, committed buyers forgive a lapse. The Kuṟaḷ says those whose friendship has grown out of love do not withdraw their love even when the friend does them harm. It describes friendship, not a customer's tie to a brand.
pairings.quote: “Those whose friendship grew from love do not give up that love even when the friend brings them ruin.” அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார் அன்பின் வழிவந்த கேண்மை யவர். Tirukkuṟaḷ 807

chapters.title: Pricing Decisions: Objectives, Factors and Strategies
chapters.scope: Why firms price as they do, what limits them, and the main pricing strategies.

blocks.title: Pricing objectives and factors
blocks.html:
Price is the amount charged for a product, or the sum of the values customers give up to have it. It is the only element of the mix that produces revenue; the others are costs. It is also the most flexible element, since it can be changed quickly, and cost, price and revenue all depend on one another.

Who sets prices. In small firms the owner often does; in large ones, division and product-line managers do, within objectives and policies set by top management. Where pricing is critical, as in aerospace, railways and oil, firms often have a pricing department. Sales, production and finance managers, and government, also influence prices.

ObjectiveWhat the firm does
SurvivalPrices just to cover variable costs and some fixed costs, to stay in business through overcapacity, intense competition or changing wants
Maximum current profitSets the price that gives the highest short-run profit
Maximum market share (penetration)Sets a low price to attract buyers quickly and gain share, expecting lower unit costs with volume
Maximum market skimmingSets a high initial price for early adopters, then lowers it over time
Product-quality leadershipPrices high to signal and pay for superior quality

Other objectives include pricing low to discourage new entrants, pricing to keep the loyalty and support of channel members, pricing for a sales promotion, and pricing one product to help the sales of others.

InternalExternal
Costs (the floor for price)Customers' perceived value and demand, including price elasticity (the ceiling)
Overall marketing objectives and positioningCompetitors' prices and offers
The rest of the marketing mixThe economy: inflation, recession, interest rates
Brand imageGovernment regulation and channel members' reactions

Costs set the floor, customer value the ceiling, competitors the range between.

blocks.title: Setting the price
blocks.html:
Consumer psychology. Economists traditionally treated consumers as ‘price takers’ who accept prices at face value. Marketers know that buyers actively interpret prices in the light of past purchases, advertising, sales calls, friends and family, and what they see at the point of sale. Buying decisions rest on how consumers perceive prices, not on the stated price. Buyers may have a lower threshold, below which a price signals poor quality, and an upper threshold, above which the product seems not worth the money.

StepWhat it involves
1 Select the pricing objectiveSurvival, maximum current profit, maximum market share, maximum market skimming or product-quality leadership
2 Determine demandDifferent prices lead to different demand, depending on the market (pure competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, pure monopoly) and on price elasticity. Demand sets the ceiling.
3 Estimate costsFixed, variable, total and average costs set the floor. In target costing the firm starts from the price the market will pay and designs the product to meet the cost that allows
4 Analyse competitors' costs, prices and offersThe three Cs: the company's costs (the floor), competitors' prices (an orienting point), and customers' perceived value (the ceiling)
5 Select a pricing methodCost-based: mark-up (cost-plus), target-return (return on investment), break-even, marginal-cost or full-cost (absorption) pricing. Value-based: perceived-value pricing, or value pricing (high quality at a fairly low price). Competition-based: going-rate or sealed-bid (auction) pricing
6 Select the final priceConsidering psychological pricing, the influence of the other mix elements, company pricing policies, and the effect on distributors, the sales force, competitors and government

Objective, demand, costs, competitors, method, final price.

blocks.title: Pricing strategies
blocks.html:
StrategyHow it worksSuits
Cost-plus (mark-up)Adds a standard mark-up to costSimple; ignores demand and competition
Target-return (break-even)Sets the price that gives a target return on investmentUtilities and regulated firms
Value-based (perceived value)Sets price from buyers' perception of value, not from costDifferentiated products
Going-rate (competition-based)Prices at or near competitors' pricesCommodities and oligopolies
PremiumPrices deliberately above the nearest competitors to signal higher qualityBrands with a quality reputation
CustomaryKeeps a price buyers have come to expect, adjusting the product rather than the priceLow-priced snacks and confectionery
Everyday low pricing (EDLP)Keeps prices consistently low, with few temporary discountsDiscount retailers
Market skimmingHigh launch price, lowered over timeInnovative products, buyers willing to pay, few competitors able to enter quickly
Market penetrationLow launch price to win share fastPrice-sensitive markets where costs fall with volume and low prices deter competitors
PsychologicalUses price perceptions: odd prices such as ₹99, reference prices, price as a signal of qualityConsumer goods
Differential (discriminatory)Different prices to different customers, product forms, places or times, not reflecting cost differencesStudents' discounts, peak and off-peak fares
BundleSeveral products together at a reduced priceCombos, packaged services

A correction. A common definition says penetration pricing means launching low and then raising the price. Penetration aims to win share with a low price; it does not require a later rise, and many penetration prices stay low.

Skim when buyers pay for novelty; penetrate when volume lowers cost.

blocks.title: Adapting the price
blocks.html:
Firms rarely set one price. They build a price structure that reflects differences in geography, segment, timing, order size, delivery, guarantees and service, so the firm seldom earns the same profit on every unit it sells. Kotler and Keller name four kinds of price adaptation.

FormHow it works
Geographical pricingDeciding what to charge customers in different places: whether to charge distant buyers more for shipping, how to handle exchange rates, and how to be paid. Methods include point-of-production (FOB-origin) pricing, where each buyer pays freight from the factory; uniform delivered pricing, the same price plus freight for everyone; zone pricing, one price within each zone; and freight-absorption pricing, where the seller bears part of the freight to win business
BarterBuyer and seller exchange goods directly, with no money and no third party
Compensation dealThe seller takes part of the payment in cash and the rest in products
Buyback arrangementThe seller supplies a plant, equipment or technology and accepts part payment in products made with it
OffsetThe seller is paid in full in cash but agrees to spend a substantial amount in that country within a set time
KindGiven for
Cash discountPaying bills promptly
Quantity discountBuying large volumes
Functional (trade) discountChannel members who perform functions such as selling, storing and record-keeping
Seasonal discountBuying out of season
AllowanceExtra payment for resellers who join special programmes, such as trade-in or promotional allowances
TechniqueHow it works
Loss-leader pricingCutting the price of well-known brands to draw traffic into the store
Special-event pricingSpecial prices in certain seasons, such as year-end offers
Special-customer pricingPrices offered only to certain customers
Cash rebatesCash back for buying within a set period
Low-interest financing and longer payment termsCheap credit, or loans stretched to lower monthly payments, instead of a price cut
Warranties and service contractsAdding free or low-cost cover
Psychological discountingSetting an artificially high reference price and offering big ‘savings’ from it; it misleads buyers if the ‘was’ price was never really charged
KindExample
Customer-segment pricingLower museum fees for students and senior citizens
Product-form pricingA large bottle of water priced lower per litre than a small one, not in proportion to cost
Image pricingThe same perfume sold at two prices in different bottles with different names and images
Channel pricingA soft drink costing more in a fine restaurant than from a vending machine
Location pricingDifferent prices for seats at a stadium, though each costs the same to provide
Time pricingPrices that vary by season, day or hour, such as peak and off-peak tariffs

Differentiated pricing is price discrimination: selling the same product at two or more prices that do not reflect differences in cost.

Psychological pricing works because buyers read a price ending just below a whole number, such as ₹399, as nearer the lower figure than the higher one.

Geography, discounts, promotions, differentiation.

blocks.title: Price-quality strategies
blocks.html:
When a firm enters a market or launches a product, it must decide where to place it on a price-quality map. Where buyers lack information about quality, they tend to take price as its signal. Kotler describes nine price-quality strategies.

Product qualityHigh priceMedium priceLow price
High1 Premium strategy2 High-value strategy3 Super-value strategy
Medium4 Overcharging strategy5 Medium-value strategy6 Good-value strategy
Low7 Rip-off strategy8 False-economy strategy9 Economy strategy

The diagonal strategies (1, 5 and 9) can coexist in the same market, one firm offering high quality at a high price and another low quality at a low price, so long as there are buyers who want each. Strategies 2, 3 and 6 attack the diagonal by offering more quality for the price. Strategies 4, 7 and 8 overprice the product for its quality; customers will feel cheated and complain, so they are hard to sustain.

Price should match quality; more quality for the price attacks, less quality for the price fails.

pairings.modern: Cost and market factors in price
text: Manu tells the king to fix the buying and selling rates of goods after weighing where they come from and where they go, how long they have been stored, and the gain and loss on them, and to review those rates publicly every five nights or every fortnight. These are the cost and market factors any price still has to reckon with, though the verse describes prices set by the ruler, not by firms.
pairings.quote: आगमं निर्गमं स्थानं तथा वृद्धिक्षयावुभौ । विचार्य सर्वपण्यानां कारयेत्क्रयविक्रयौ । āgamaṃ nirgamaṃ sthānaṃ tathā vṛddhikṣayāv ubhau / vicārya sarvapaṇyānāṃ kārayet krayavikrayau. “After weighing the arrival and dispatch, the storage, and the gain and loss of all goods, he should fix their buying and selling prices.” Manusmṛti 8.401; review at 8.402

chapters.title: Place: Distribution Channels, Logistics and Supply Chains
chapters.scope: How products reach customers: the channels they pass through, the logistics that move them, and the supply chain behind them.

blocks.title: Distribution channels
blocks.html:
A distribution channel (marketing channel, trade channel) is the set of interdependent organisations that make a product available for use or consumption, transferring ownership from the point of production to the point of consumption. Choosing channels is among the most complex decisions a firm faces. Channels form part of a wider value network: the system of partnerships and alliances a firm creates to source, augment and deliver its offerings.

KindRoleExamples
MerchantsBuy, take title to and resell the goodsWholesalers, retailers
AgentsSearch for customers and may negotiate for the producer, but do not take titleBrokers, manufacturers' representatives, sales agents
FacilitatorsAssist distribution but neither take title nor negotiateTransport firms, independent warehouses, banks, advertising agencies

Channel functions. Channel members gather information about customers and competitors; develop and spread persuasive communications; negotiate price and terms; place orders; finance inventories; bear the risks of channel work; store and move products; arrange payment through banks; and oversee the transfer of ownership. They smooth the flow of goods and save the producer money, time and effort.

TypeHow it works
DirectThe producer sells straight to the final customer, without intermediaries
IndirectThe producer uses intermediaries such as wholesalers and retailers
Hybrid (multichannel)The producer combines direct and indirect channels for reach and convenience
LevelPath
Zero-level (direct)Producer → consumer
One-levelProducer → retailer → consumer
Two-levelProducer → wholesaler → retailer → consumer
Three-levelProducer → wholesaler → jobber or agent → retailer → consumer
IntensityNumber of outletsTypical goods
IntensiveAs many as possibleConvenience goods: soap, biscuits, soft drinks
SelectiveMore than one but fewer than all willing dealersShopping goods: appliances, furniture
ExclusiveOne or very few dealers in each areaSpecialty and luxury goods: premium cars, designer labels

Direct or through intermediaries; intensive, selective or exclusive.

blocks.title: Channel systems and push and pull
blocks.html:
In a conventional channel, producer, wholesaler and retailer are separate businesses each maximising its own profit, often at the others' expense, which breeds conflict. A vertical marketing system (VMS) makes them act as one unified system.

KindHow the channel is unified
CorporateOne member owns the others, though each stage keeps its own task
ContractualIndependent firms join by contract: wholesaler-sponsored voluntary chains, retailer cooperatives (retailers buying through a jointly owned wholesaler) and franchise organisations
AdministeredOne member is large and powerful enough to coordinate the others without owning them

Franchises themselves take three forms: manufacturer-sponsored retailer franchises (as with car dealers), manufacturer-sponsored wholesaler franchises (as with soft-drink bottlers licensed to bottle and distribute) and service-firm-sponsored retailer franchises (as with fast-food chains). Most short accounts mention only the second.

A VMS resembles vertical integration, in which a firm takes over the next link in the chain, forward toward customers or backward toward suppliers.

A horizontal marketing system joins two or more unrelated companies at the same level of the channel to exploit an opportunity, pooling capital, skills or marketing resources, often through a joint venture or alliance, temporary or permanent. It is sometimes called a merger, but it is cooperation, and the firms usually stay separate.

Multichannel (hybrid) marketing reaches customer segments through two or more channels at once: stores, websites, catalogues, direct mail, email and mobile.

StrategyHow it worksSuits
PushThe manufacturer uses its sales force and trade promotions to induce intermediaries to carry, promote and sell the productLow brand loyalty, brand chosen in the store, impulse items, well-understood benefits
PullThe manufacturer uses advertising and promotion to make consumers ask intermediaries for the productHigh brand loyalty and involvement, clear differences between brands, brand chosen before the store visit

Reverse-flow channels move goods back from users to reuse products or containers, refurbish them for resale, recycle them, or dispose of products and packaging, through redemption centres, community groups, recycling centres and brokers. Service channels keep multiplying too: banks, insurers and travel firms serve customers through branches, phones and the internet, and performers and politicians reach their audiences through mass media, rallies, social networks and their own websites.

Conventional, vertical, horizontal, multichannel; push through the trade or pull through consumers.

blocks.title: Market logistics
blocks.html:
Market logistics, also called physical distribution or marketing logistics, is planning, implementing and controlling the physical flow of materials, final goods and related information from points of origin to points of use, to meet customer requirements at a profit. Peter Drucker called distribution “the economy's dark continent” (1962) for the savings it hid; physical distribution has since grown into supply chain management. Physical distribution starts at the factory, where managers choose stocking points and carriers to deliver goods on time or at the lowest total cost; supply chain management starts earlier, with procuring the right inputs (raw materials, components, capital equipment) and converting them efficiently into finished products.

Kotler and Keller report that the total cost of market logistics can amount to 30 to 40 per cent of a product's cost, which is why many experts call it ‘the last frontier for cost economies’: lower logistics costs allow lower prices, higher margins, or both.

TypeFlowAim
InboundRaw materials and inputs from suppliers to the factory and warehouse: procurement, receiving, storageSmooth production
OutboundFinished goods from the warehouse to customers and retailers: order processing, picking, packing, shippingCustomer satisfaction
ReverseReturns, recalls, repairs, recycling and excess stock back through the chainRecover value and build trust

Inbound logistics deals with supply and outbound logistics fulfils demand. Inbound runs from supplier or manufacturer to the company, its warehouse or a third-party logistics firm: purchasing, receiving and stowing goods with inventory tracking, and processing returns (reverse logistics is often handled as part of inbound). Outbound runs from the company to the customer: order processing in a warehouse management system, picking and packing, and shipping.

The flow of market logistics. A sales forecast sets the schedules for distribution, production and inventory; production plans tell purchasing what materials to order; materials arrive by inbound transport and are stored; they are converted into finished goods, whose inventory links customer orders to manufacturing; finished goods then pass through packaging, warehousing, shipping, outbound transport, field warehousing and delivery.

DecisionKey question
Order processingHow quickly can we go from order to payment?
WarehousingHow many warehouses, and where?
InventoryWhen to reorder (the reorder point) and how much (the order quantity)?
TransportationWhich mode, judged by cost, speed and reliability?

Trade-offs. The ideal is the right goods in the right place at the right time at the lowest cost, but no system can both maximise service and minimise cost. Higher service needs more inventory and faster transport; less inventory risks stockouts; cheaper packaging risks damage; rail is cheaper than air but slower, tying up working capital and delaying payment. Because these costs interact, often in opposite directions, decisions must be made on a total-system basis, starting from what customers require and what competitors offer. The aim is to maximise profit, not sales: some firms offer less service at a lower price, others more service at a premium.

Kotler and Keller plan market logistics in four steps: decide the value proposition to customers (delivery speed, accuracy, billing); choose the channel design and network (direct or through intermediaries, how many warehouses and where); develop operational excellence in forecasting, warehousing, transport and materials; and implement with information systems, equipment, policies and continuous improvement. An integrated logistics system ties materials management, material flow and physical distribution together with technology such as point-of-sale data, barcodes, electronic data interchange (EDI), electronic funds transfer and satellite tracking.

Right goods, right place, right time, lowest cost: trade-offs throughout.

blocks.title: The four logistics decisions
blocks.html:
DecisionWhat it involves
Order processingShortening the order-to-payment cycle: order transmission, order entry and credit check, inventory and production scheduling, shipping the order and invoice, and receiving payment. The longer the cycle, the lower customer satisfaction and profit.
WarehousingStoring goods because production and consumption rarely coincide. More stocking locations speed delivery but raise warehousing and inventory costs, so firms often centralise stock and use fast transport. Warehouses may be private or public; storage warehouses hold goods for moderate to long periods, while distribution warehouses move goods out as soon as possible; automated warehouses are run by a central computer. Some warehouses now assemble and pack, postponing final configuration to match demand more closely.
InventoryInventory cost rises at an accelerating rate as the service level approaches 100 per cent. The order (reorder) point balances the risk of stockout against the cost of overstock; the order quantity balances order-processing costs (set-up and running costs) against carrying costs (storage, capital, taxes and insurance, depreciation and obsolescence), which Kotler and Keller put as high as 30 per cent of inventory value. Larger stocks must earn incremental gross profit above their incremental carrying cost.
TransportationMode choice affects price, on-time delivery and the condition of goods. Shippers weigh speed, frequency, dependability, capability, availability, traceability and cost. For speed, air, rail and road lead; for low cost, water and pipeline.
CarrierMeaning
PrivateThe shipper owns its own fleet of trucks or aircraft
ContractAn independent firm selling transport to others on contract
CommonA carrier serving set routes on a schedule, open to all shippers at standard rates

Order processing, warehousing, inventory, transportation.

blocks.title: Supply chain management
blocks.html:
AspectLogisticsSupply chain management (SCM)
ScopeMovement and storage of goods, mainly within one organisationThe whole chain from procurement through manufacturing to distribution
RelationA part of SCMThe wider whole
CoordinationInternalAcross many organisations
GoalEfficient logistics operations and customer satisfactionCompetitive advantage through an efficient, responsive chain
OriginThe older conceptThe newer, wider concept that grew out of logistics

A supply chain is the connected network of people, organisations, resources, activities and technologies involved in making and selling a product, from raw materials reaching the manufacturer to the finished product reaching the consumer. Supply chain management coordinates these activities, streamlining the supply side to maximise customer value and gain competitive advantage. Controlling manufacturing improves quality and reduces the risk of recalls and lawsuits; controlling shipping avoids costly shortages and oversupply; both raise margins, especially for large international firms.

The Supply Chain Council's SCOR model names five core processes: plan, source, make, deliver and return. Good SCM improves quality and customer service, reduces risk, raises profitability, and helps suppliers and buyers innovate together, as at Amazon, Flipkart, P&G, PepsiCo and Nestlé.

DriverFor responsivenessFor efficiency
ProductionExcess capacity, flexible methods, many smaller plantsLittle excess capacity, specialised plants
InventoryHigh stock of a wide rangeLow stock of a narrower range
LocationMany facilities close to customersFew central facilities serving wide areas
TransportationFrequent shipments by fast, flexible modesFewer, larger shipments by slower, cheaper modes
InformationTimely, accurate data shared widelyLower information costs

Green supply chain practices include route optimisation, consolidating shipments, recyclable packaging and cutting the carbon footprint.

Plan, source, make, deliver, return; responsive or efficient.

text: The Arthaśāstra's superintendent of the storehouse is told to keep half of the stored stock in reserve against calamities for the people, to use the other half, and to replace old stock with new. Safety stock and stock rotation are the same disciplines in modern inventory management.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.15

text: Kauṭilya compares trade routes. Earlier teachers preferred water routes as cheaper and easier; Kauṭilya prefers land routes as less liable to obstruction and danger, and among land routes he prefers the southern one for the goods it yields in quantity. Weighing routes by cost, risk and what they deliver is the same reasoning as a supply chain's choice of transport.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 7.12

text: The Jain Tattvārtha Sūtra states that living beings render service to one another. Supply chain management rests on a commercial version of the same idea: suppliers, makers and distributors do better by coordinating than by squeezing each other. The sūtra is a statement about all life, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Living beings render service to one another.” परस्परोपग्रहो जीवानाम् । parasparopagraho jīvānām. Umāsvāti, Tattvārtha Sūtra 5.21

chapters.title: Promotion Decisions: The Communication Mix and Budget
chapters.scope: The tools a firm uses to communicate with its market, how they are combined, and how the budget is set.

blocks.title: The promotion mix
blocks.html:
Marketing communications are the means by which firms inform, persuade and remind consumers, directly or indirectly, about the products and brands they sell. They are the voice of the company and its brands, and a way to build a dialogue and relationships with consumers; for consumers, they show how and why a product is used, by whom, where and when. The promotion mix (marketing communications mix) is the blend of tools a company uses for this. Its objectives are to inform, persuade, remind and, in social causes, modify behaviour.

ToolMeaningStrengths
AdvertisingAny paid form of non-personal presentation of ideas, goods or services by an identified sponsorReaches large audiences at low cost per exposure; builds image
Sales promotionShort-term incentives to encourage purchase: coupons, discounts, contests, samplesQuick response; boosts short-term sales
Personal sellingPersonal presentation by the sales force to make sales and build relationshipsTwo-way, adaptable; best at the stage of conviction and purchase
Public relationsBuilding good relations with the public through publicity, events and handling of storiesCredible; reaches people who avoid advertising
Direct and digital marketingDirect connections with targeted individuals: mail, email, phone, SMS, online and mobileTargeted, immediate, measurable

Kotler and Keller (14th edition) list eight modes: advertising, sales promotion, events and experiences, public relations and publicity, direct marketing, interactive (online) marketing, word-of-mouth marketing and personal selling. Later editions fold the online modes into online and social media marketing and mobile marketing.

Integrated marketing communications (IMC), in the AMA's definition, is “a planning process designed to assure that all brand contacts received by a customer or prospect for a product, service, or organization are relevant to that person and consistent over time”. It takes a ‘360-degree view’ of the consumer, makes someone responsible for unifying the brand's messages, and aims to reach the right customers with the right messages at the right time and place. Integrated marketing more broadly means designing every activity with all the others in mind, so that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.

StrategyHow it worksMain tools
PushThe producer promotes to channel members, who promote to final buyersPersonal selling and trade promotion
PullThe producer promotes to final consumers, who ask channel members for the productAdvertising and consumer promotion

AIDA (attention, interest, desire, action), usually credited to E. St. Elmo Lewis (1898), is the oldest model of how buyers respond to communication.

Advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, PR, direct marketing.

blocks.title: Developing effective communications
blocks.html:
StepWhat it involves
1 Identify the target audiencePotential buyers, current users, deciders and influencers; individuals, groups, particular publics or the general public
2 Determine the objectivesAt any level of the hierarchy of effects (see below)
3 Design the communicationsWhat to say (message strategy), how to say it (creative strategy) and who should say it (message source)
4 Select the channelsPersonal and non-personal channels
5 Establish the total budgetAffordable, percentage-of-sales, competitive-parity or objective-and-task
6 Decide on the communications mixAllocate the budget across the modes
7 Measure results and manage IMCCheck effects and keep the messages integrated
ObjectiveMeaning
Category needEstablish the need for the category, as any new-to-the-world product such as early electric cars must
Brand awarenessHelp consumers recognise or recall the brand within the category; recognition is easier to achieve than recall
Brand attitudeHelp consumers judge the brand's ability to meet a relevant need: problem-solution appeals for cleaning products, sensory appeals for foods
Brand purchase intentionMove consumers to decide to buy, or to take a purchase-related action

Message, creative and source. The message strategy looks for appeals and themes that tie to the brand's positioning and its points of parity and difference. Creative strategy uses informational appeals, which elaborate on attributes and benefits (problem-solution, demonstration, comparison and testimonial ads), or transformational appeals, which elaborate on a non-product benefit or image, such as what kind of person uses the brand. Attractive or popular sources win more attention and recall, which is why firms use celebrities.

ChannelForms
PersonalTwo or more people communicating directly, face to face, by phone or online, allowing individual presentation and feedback: advocate channels (company salespeople), expert channels (independent experts) and social channels (neighbours, friends, family)
Non-personal (mass)Communications directed to more than one person: media (print, broadcast, electronic, display), atmospheres (packaged environments that reinforce leanings toward a product) and events

Audience, objectives, design, channels, budget, mix, results.

blocks.title: Setting the promotion budget
blocks.html:
MethodHow it worksWeakness
AffordableSpend what the company thinks it can afford after other costsIgnores promotion's effect on sales; budget varies year to year
Percentage of salesSpend a set percentage of current or forecast salesTreats sales as the cause of promotion rather than its result
Competitive parityMatch competitors' spendingCompetitors' needs and wisdom may differ
Objective and taskDefine objectives, set the tasks to achieve them, cost the tasks; the total is the budgetDemanding to estimate, but the most logical

The difficulty is captured in a saying usually credited to the retailer John Wanamaker: half the money spent on advertising is wasted; the trouble is knowing which half. In competitive parity, firms aim at share-of-voice parity with rivals.

Objective and task is the most logical method.

blocks.title: Advertising
blocks.html:
Advertising is any paid form of non-personal presentation and promotion of ideas, goods or services by an identified sponsor. It reaches geographically dispersed buyers, can build a long-term image or trigger quick sales, and may affect sales simply by its presence. Its qualities are public presentation, pervasiveness (the message can be repeated many times), amplified expressiveness (dramatising the brand through print, sound and colour), impersonality, and control over what the message stresses.

Its forms include print and broadcast ads, outer packaging and inserts, cinema, posters and leaflets, brochures, directories, billboards, point-of-purchase displays, advertorials, infomercials, and online banner, video and social media ads.

MDecision
MissionSetting the objectives
MoneyDeciding the budget
MessageGenerating, evaluating and executing the message, and checking its social responsibility
MediaChoosing reach, frequency and impact, the media types and vehicles, and timing
MeasurementEvaluating the communication and sales effects
KindAim
InformativeCreate awareness and knowledge of new products or features
PersuasiveCreate liking, preference, conviction and purchase
ReminderStimulate repeat purchase
ReinforcementConvince current buyers they made the right choice

Budget factors: the stage in the product life cycle, market share and consumer base, competition and clutter, the advertising frequency needed, and how substitutable the product is. Although treated as a current expense, part of advertising is an investment in brand equity.

Media. Media selection finds the most cost-effective media to deliver the desired number and type of exposures: reach (how many people are exposed at least once), frequency (how often the average person is exposed) and impact (the qualitative value of an exposure). As traditional mass media lose effectiveness, advertisers use more alternative media. Effectiveness is measured both as a communication effect (on awareness, knowledge or preference) and as a sales effect.

Mission, money, message, media, measurement.

blocks.title: Sales promotion and personal selling
blocks.html:
Sales promotion is a set of mostly short-term incentives to encourage trial or purchase: consumer promotions, trade promotions, and business and sales-force promotions. It offers three benefits: it draws attention, gives an incentive, and makes an invitation to buy now.

Why it has grown: the growing power of retailers, declining brand loyalty, consumers' greater sensitivity to promotions, the proliferation of brands, fragmented markets, a short-term focus, demands for measurable results, and competition.

ToolWhat it is
SamplesA free amount of the product, delivered, mailed, picked up or attached to another product
CouponsCertificates entitling the bearer to a stated saving
Cash refunds (rebates)A price reduction after purchase, on proof of purchase
Price packsReduced-price packs (two for the price of one) or banded packs (a toothbrush with toothpaste)
PremiumsMerchandise free or at low cost as an incentive to buy
Frequency programmesRewards linked to how often and how much a customer buys
PrizesContests (judged entries), sweepstakes (draws) and games
Patronage awardsValue in proportion to patronage, such as reward points
Free trials, warrantiesTrying the product at no cost; promises of performance or refund
Tie-ins and cross-promotionsBrands teaming up on offers, or one brand advertising a non-competing brand
Point-of-purchase displays and demonstrationsAt the place of sale
ToolWhat it is
Price-off (off-invoice)A straight discount off the list price on each case bought in a stated period
AllowancePayment for featuring the product: an advertising allowance, or a display allowance for a special display
Free goodsExtra cases for intermediaries who buy a certain quantity
AdvantagesDisadvantages
Two-way: instant feedback lets the seller adapt the presentationExpensive per contact
Builds trust, which matters for high-value productsLabour-intensive; needs a large sales force
More persuasive: a buyer face to face is less likely to dismiss the sellerTraining is slow and costly
Reaches buyers other methods cannotReaches relatively few people

Sales promotion buys action now; personal selling builds conviction one buyer at a time.

text: Advertising aims to hold its audience and reach even those not yet listening. The Kuṟaḷ describes true speech as speech that binds its hearers and makes even those who were not listening want to hear. It is about eloquence, not paid media.
pairings.quote: “True speech binds those who hear it and makes even those who did not hear it long for it.” கேட்டார்ப் பிணிக்கும் தகையவாய்க் கேளாரும் வேட்ப மொழிவதாம் சொல். Tirukkuṟaḷ 643

text: The affordable method sets spending by what the firm can bear. The Kuṟaḷ says to give according to the measure of one's means: that is the way to give while keeping one's wealth. The couplet concerns a ruler's or householder's gifts, not a promotion budget.
pairings.quote: “Give with knowledge of the measure of your means; that is the way to give while guarding your wealth.” ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து ஈக அதுபொருள் போற்றி வழங்கு நெறி. Tirukkuṟaḷ 477

chapters.title: Consumer and Industrial Buying Behaviour
chapters.scope: Why and how people and organisations buy: the influences on them, the decision process, the rules they use, and how business buying differs.

blocks.title: Consumer behaviour and its influences
blocks.html:
Consumer behaviour is the study of how individuals, groups and organisations select, buy, use and dispose of goods, services, ideas or experiences to satisfy their needs and wants (Kotler). Leon Schiffman and Leslie Lazar Kanuk define it as the behaviour consumers display in searching for, purchasing, using, evaluating and disposing of products and services that they expect will satisfy their needs. It draws on psychology, sociology, anthropology and economics, and is complex, dynamic, goal-oriented and shaped by perception.

FactorVariablesNotes
CulturalCulture, subculture, social classCulture is the most basic cause of wants; subcultures (ethnic, religious, regional) form niche markets; class shapes lifestyle and access
SocialReference groups, family, roles and statusPrimary groups (family, friends) and secondary groups (professional bodies) shape attitudes; buying roles are initiator, influencer, decider, buyer and user
PersonalAge and life-cycle stage, occupation, economic situation, lifestyle, personality and self-conceptLifestyle is measured by activities, interests and opinions (AIO)
PsychologicalMotivation, perception, learning, beliefs and attitudesMaslow's and Herzberg's theories; selective attention, distortion and retention; learning by experience; attitudes are lasting and hard to change

Cultural, social, personal, psychological.

blocks.title: The buying decision process
blocks.html:
StageWhat happens
1 Need recognitionThe buyer recognises a gap between the actual and the desired state, triggered by internal stimuli (hunger) or external ones (an advertisement)
2 Information searchInternal search of memory and experience; external search among family, friends, experts, reviews and advertising
3 Evaluation of alternativesComparing options on criteria such as price, brand, features and quality, within the evoked set
4 Purchase decisionForming an intention and buying; others' attitudes and unexpected situations can intervene
5 Post-purchase behaviourSatisfaction leads to repurchase and loyalty; dissatisfaction to returns and complaints

The evoked set. From the total set of brands available, a buyer is aware of some (the awareness set), considers fewer (the consideration or evoked set), and chooses among a few (the choice set).

Cognitive dissonance (Leon Festinger, 1957) is the discomfort after purchase caused by doubt about the choice, often called buyer's remorse. Marketers reduce it with reassurance, guarantees and after-sales contact. Satisfaction depends on the gap between expectations and perceived performance.

Involvement decides how much of this process a buyer goes through, from routine to extensive decisions.

Need, search, evaluate, buy, reflect.

blocks.title: Types of buying behaviour
blocks.html:
Henry Assael classified buying behaviour by the buyer's involvement and the differences between brands.

Brand differencesHigh involvementLow involvement
Significant differences between brandsComplex buying: buying a car. The marketer gives detailed information and trials.Variety-seeking: soft drinks, biscuits. Buyers switch for variety; leaders keep shelf space and remind, challengers offer deals and novelty.
Few differences between brandsDissonance-reducing: buying a carpet. The marketer provides reassurance and after-sales support.Habitual: salt. Buyers buy by habit; marketers use price, promotion and repetition to build familiarity.

High involvement and real differences make buying complex.
