blocks.title: Decision rules and models of buyer behaviour
blocks.html:
RuleHow the buyer choosesMarketing implication
ConjunctiveSets a minimum acceptable level on every attribute and chooses the first brand that meets all of themMake sure the product meets the minimum on everything
DisjunctiveSets a high standard on one or a few key attributes and accepts a brand that meets any of themHighlight a standout feature
LexicographicRanks the attributes and compares brands on the most important first, moving to the next only if there is a tieExcel on the attribute buyers rank first

These rules are non-compensatory: a weakness on one attribute cannot be made up by strength on another. Under compensatory rules, such as Martin Fishbein's expectancy-value model, a buyer weighs all attributes together, so strengths can offset weaknesses.

TypeExplains buying by…
Economic (Marshallian)Rational choice to maximise satisfaction within a budget
PsychologicalLearning and conditioning (Pavlovian), unconscious motives (Freudian), needs (Maslow)
Sociological (Veblenian)Family, social class, reference groups and culture
ComprehensiveCombining these: the Nicosia model (1966), the Engel–Kollat–Blackwell model (1968) and the Howard–Sheth model (1969)

Conjunctive: every minimum. Disjunctive: one high standard. Lexicographic: the top attribute first.

blocks.title: Industrial (organisational) buying behaviour
blocks.html:
Organisational buying, in Frederick Webster and Yoram Wind's definition, is the decision-making process by which formal organisations establish the need for purchased products and services, and identify, evaluate and choose among alternative brands and suppliers.

How business markets differ: fewer, larger buyers; close supplier-customer relationships; professional purchasing by trained buyers; several people influencing each decision; geographically concentrated buyers; and derived demand: demand for business goods comes from demand for the consumer goods they help produce, so it is fairly inelastic in the short run and fluctuates more.

BuyclassWhat happensRisk
Straight rebuyRoutine reorder from an established supplier with little evaluationLow
Modified rebuyThe buyer re-evaluates products, prices or suppliers because needs have changedMedium
New taskA first-time purchase needing extensive research and many decision-makersHigh

The buyclasses and the buygrid come from Patrick Robinson, Charles Faris and Yoram Wind (Industrial Buying and Creative Marketing, 1967). The buygrid crosses the three buyclasses with eight buyphases: problem recognition, general need description, product specification, supplier search, proposal solicitation, supplier selection, order-routine specification, and performance review.

The buying centre is everyone involved in a purchase decision. Webster and Wind (1972) named five roles: users, influencers, buyers, deciders and gatekeepers (who control the flow of information); later writers add initiators and approvers. Their model groups the influences on organisational buying into four kinds: environmental, organisational, interpersonal and individual.

Straight rebuy, modified rebuy, new task.

text: The Kuṟaḷ says that just as water changes its nature with the soil it flows through, people's understanding takes on the nature of the company they keep. That is the reference group effect: the groups we belong to and look to shape what we think and want.
pairings.quote: “As water changes with the nature of the soil, so a person's understanding takes the nature of their company.” நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர்திரிந் தற்றாகும் மாந்தர்க்கு இனத்தியல்ப தாகும் அறிவு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 452

text: Cognitive dissonance is regret after a choice. The Kuṟaḷ warns against doing what will later make one cry, ‘what have I done?’, and if it has been done, not to do it again. It speaks of wrong actions generally, not purchases.
pairings.quote: “Do nothing that will make you grieve, ‘what have I done!’; and if you have, better not do such things again.” எற்றென்று இரங்குவ செய்யற்க செய்வானேல் மற்றன்ன செய்யாமை நன்று. Tirukkuṟaḷ 655

text: The Arthaśāstra devotes a chapter to examining precious goods, gems, pearls and the like, before they are accepted into the treasury, with their qualities and defects set out so that experts can judge them. Professional, specification-based examination of what an organisation buys is the same practice in an industrial buying centre.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.11

chapters.title: Services Marketing
chapters.scope: How services differ from goods, the extended marketing mix, how service quality is measured, and the three kinds of services marketing.

blocks.title: Services and their characteristics
blocks.html:
A service is any act or performance one party offers another that is essentially intangible and does not result in the ownership of anything (Kotler). Services marketing creates value through experiences, processes and interactions; it is relationship-oriented, and customer interaction is critical.

CharacteristicMeaningExampleMarketing response
IntangibilityCannot be seen, tasted, felt or heard before purchaseInsurance, legal adviceMake it tangible with evidence: facilities, staff, testimonials
InseparabilityProduced and consumed at the same time; the provider is part of the serviceA doctor's consultationTrain the people who deliver it; manage customers' participation
Variability (heterogeneity)Quality depends on who provides it, when, where and howRestaurant serviceStandardise processes, train staff, track satisfaction
PerishabilityCannot be stored for later sale or use; unused capacity is lostEmpty airline seatsMatch supply and demand: differential pricing, reservations, part-time staff
Lack of ownershipThe customer gets an experience or access, not ownershipEducation, tourismBuild membership and loyalty
CategoryExample
Pure tangible goodSoap, toothpaste or salt, with no accompanying service
Tangible good with accompanying servicesA car, computer or phone; the more advanced the product, the more it needs good support
HybridA restaurant meal: equal parts goods and service
Major service with accompanying minor goods and servicesAir travel, with snacks and drinks
Pure serviceBabysitting, psychotherapy, massage

Managing the characteristics. Because buyers cannot see a service in advance, they look for evidence of quality in the place, people, equipment, communication material, symbols and price, so the provider's task is to manage the evidence and ‘tangibilise the intangible’. Variability can be reduced in three steps: invest in good hiring and training, standardise the service process across the organisation, and monitor customer satisfaction; service guarantees reassure buyers. Perishability matters when demand fluctuates: transport firms must own enough equipment for rush hour, and some doctors charge for missed appointments. Demand or yield management aims to offer the right services to the right customers at the right places, times and prices.

Intangible, inseparable, variable, perishable, not owned.

blocks.title: The services marketing mix: 7Ps
blocks.html:
Bernard Booms and Mary Jo Bitner (1981) added three Ps to the four for services.

PFocusExample
ProductThe core and supplementary servicesA bank loan
PriceValue-based and flexible pricingA subscription fee
PlaceAccessibility and deliveryBranches and mobile apps
PromotionCommunicationAdvertising, public relations
PeopleEveryone who takes part in delivering the serviceReceptionists, agents
ProcessThe procedures and flow by which the service is deliveredA booking system
Physical evidenceThe setting and tangible cuesOffices, uniforms, brochures

The 4Ps plus people, process and physical evidence.

blocks.title: Service quality and SERVQUAL
blocks.html:
SERVQUAL (A. Parasuraman, Valarie Zeithaml and Leonard Berry, 1988) measures service quality as the gap between customers' expectations and their perceptions of performance, on five dimensions. It grew out of the same authors' gaps model (1985).

DimensionMeaningExample
ReliabilityPerforming the promised service dependably and accuratelyOn-time delivery
AssuranceEmployees' knowledge and courtesy, and their ability to convey trust and confidenceSkilled, courteous staff
TangiblesThe appearance of physical facilities, equipment, staff and materialsA modern office
EmpathyCaring, individual attentionPersonalised care
ResponsivenessWillingness to help customers and give prompt serviceQuick support
GapBetweenExample
1 Knowledge gapCustomers' expectations and management's perception of themA bank's managers think customers want better debit cards when they care more about staff responsiveness
2 Standards gapManagement's perceptions and the service quality specificationsManagers ask tellers for ‘fast’ service without saying how many minutes
3 Delivery gapThe specifications and the service actually deliveredStaff are poorly trained, or caught between standards such as listening to customers and serving them fast
4 Communication gapThe service delivered and what is promised to customersA hospital brochure shows a beautiful room; the patient finds a shabby one
5 Customer gapExpected and perceived service; the result of gaps 1 to 4A doctor's frequent visits, meant to show care, make the patient think something is wrong

Customers form expectations from past experience, word of mouth and advertising, and compare the service they perceive with the service they expected. Falling short disappoints; exceeding expectations delights. Kotler and Keller list the five dimensions in order of importance to customers: reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy, tangibles.

The zone of tolerance (Zeithaml, Berry and Parasuraman, 1993) is the range between the desired and the adequate service level, within which variation in service goes largely unnoticed.

ModelSatisfaction depends on…
Expectancy disconfirmation (Richard Oliver, 1980)Comparing performance with expectations: performance above expectation satisfies, below it dissatisfies
Performance-onlyPerformance alone; useful for new services where customers have few expectations
Rational expectationsExpectations formed by logical evaluation, then matched against performance
Expectations as artefactThe expectations themselves, which shape how performance is perceived; managing expectations improves satisfaction

Reliability, Assurance, Tangibles, Empathy, Responsiveness.

blocks.title: The service triangle
blocks.html:
The service triangle links the company, its employees and its customers. Each side is a kind of marketing, and all three are needed for good service.

KindBetweenFocus
Internal marketingCompany and employeesHiring, training and motivating staff to serve customers well; building a service culture
External marketingCompany and customersPreparing, pricing, distributing and promoting the service: making promises
Interactive marketingEmployees and customersThe service encounter, where promises are kept or broken and relationships are built

Kotler and Keller argue that the marketing department's most important contribution may be to be ‘exceptionally clever in getting everyone else in the organization to practice marketing’. In interactive marketing, clients judge both technical quality (was the surgery successful?) and functional quality (did the surgeon show concern and inspire confidence?).

Internal, external, interactive: promise, enable, deliver.

blocks.title: Excellence in services and service brands
blocks.html:
Well-managed service companies share several practices (Kotler and Keller).

PracticeWhat it means
A strategic conceptBeing ‘customer-obsessed’: a clear sense of target customers and their needs, and a distinctive strategy to satisfy them; very selective hiring; some hotels keep a ‘guest historian’ to track preferences
Top-management commitmentLooking at service performance as well as financial results; McDonald's measures every outlet on QSCV: quality, service, cleanliness and value
High standardsSetting precise, appropriately high standards, such as answering calls within a set number of seconds
Profit tiersPampering high-value customers and charging more or serving more economically those who barely pay their way
Monitoring systemsAuditing their own and competitors' service: voice-of-the-customer measures, comparison and mystery shopping, surveys, suggestion and complaint forms, service-audit teams
Satisfying complaintsKotler and Keller note that on average 40 per cent of customers who have a bad service experience stop doing business with the firm; a complaint handled well is a gift, and firms that encourage complaints and empower staff to fix problems on the spot earn more

Service brands. As firms move from making products to delivering solutions and services, they build service brands, which depend on consistently high delivery; a pure service brand, such as an airline, sells mainly a service. Marketers must turn intangible services into concrete benefits and a well-defined experience, as theme parks do. Brand experience has four dimensions: sensory, affective, behavioural and intellectual.

Customer-obsessed, committed, high standards, tiers, monitoring, complaints welcomed.

text: SERVQUAL's responsiveness is the willingness to help promptly. The Kuṟaḷ says that help given at the right time, however small, is greater than the world. It is about kindness between people, not about service firms.
pairings.quote: “Help given in time of need, though small in itself, is far greater than the world.” காலத்தி னாற்செய்த நன்றி சிறிதெனினும் ஞாலத்தின் மாணப் பெரிது. Tirukkuṟaḷ 102

text: Interactive marketing happens in the moment of contact. The Kuṟaḷ says the anicham flower withers when smelt, but a guest withers at a mere cold look. It concerns a host's hospitality, which is also the root idea of the service encounter.
pairings.quote: “The anicham flower withers when smelt; a guest withers when the host's face turns cold.” மோப்பக் குழையும் அனிச்சம் முகந்திரிந்து நோக்கக் குழையும் விருந்து. Tirukkuṟaḷ 90

chapters.title: Customer Relationship Marketing
chapters.scope: Building lasting customer relationships: relationship marketing and CRM, one-to-one and permission marketing, retention and loyalty, and the CRM value chain.

blocks.title: Relationship marketing and CRM
blocks.html:
Relationship marketing, a term Leonard Berry introduced in 1983, builds long-term relationships with customers, employees and partners rather than focusing on single transactions. Its aims are customer retention, long-term engagement, loyalty and higher profitability.

AspectCustomer relationship marketing (CRMk)Customer relationship management (CRM)
What it isA strategy focused on long-term relationships rather than one-time salesA technology-driven system for managing customer interactions and data
ProvidesDirection: whom to keep and howA central customer database, personalised communication, better service

Relationship marketing is the strategy: retention goals, public relations, marketing and advertising. CRM covers the operational tasks that support it. Kotler and Keller define customer relationship management as the process of carefully managing detailed information about individual customers and all customer touch points to maximise loyalty. A hotel's touch points include reservations, check-in and check-out, frequent-stay programmes, room service, business services, the gym, laundry, restaurants and bars.

Thoughtful firms turn customers into clients: customers may be nameless, served as part of a mass or segment by whoever is available; clients cannot be nameless, and are served individually by the professional assigned to them.

CRM records every customer touch point, any occasion on which a customer meets the brand: marketing emails, service calls, website visits, store visits and loyalty programmes. The internet has moved marketing from mass marketing to personalised marketing through email, websites, call centres and databases.

Why retention matters. Keeping customers usually costs less than winning new ones. Frederick Reichheld and W. Earl Sasser (1990) found that cutting customer defections by 5 per cent could raise profits by 25 to 85 per cent, depending on the industry. Customer lifetime value (CLV) is the present value of the profits a customer will bring over the whole relationship; churn is the rate at which customers leave.

CRMk is the strategy; CRM is the technology.

blocks.title: One-to-one and permission marketing
blocks.html:
One-to-one marketing (Don Peppers and Martha Rogers, The One to One Future, 1993) treats each customer as a segment of one. Their IDIC model has four steps, and suits complex products that need continuing engagement.

StepFocus
IdentifyKnow each customer individually; build the customer database
DifferentiateRank customers by their value (CLV) and their needs
InteractEngage customers in personalised, cost-efficient dialogue
CustomiseTailor products, services and messages to each customer

Permission marketing (Seth Godin, 1999) asks for the customer's consent before sending marketing messages, so that communication is anticipated, personal and relevant; it is the opposite of interruption marketing. In participatory marketing, customers help to develop and promote products. Empowered customers now act as co-creators, advocates and content creators; friends and family remain the strongest source of influence, followed by online reviews and influencers.

In the IDIC model, firms spend proportionately more effort on their most valuable customers (MVCs), found by estimating customer lifetime value: the net present value of future profits from purchases, margins and referrals, less customer-specific service costs. One-to-one marketing suits firms that collect much individual customer data and sell many products that can be cross-sold, need periodic replacement or upgrading, and are of high value; for others, the investment may exceed the payoff.

Permission marketing assumes consumers know what they want; when their preferences are vague or conflicting, participatory marketing, in which firm and consumer work out together how best to satisfy the consumer, may fit better. Not every consumer wants to be involved with every brand, and even then only some of the time.

Reviews and recommendations. ‘Recommended by a relative or friend’ remains the strongest influence on choice, but online ratings and reviews matter more and more, and some stores display them. Bloggers and influencers with large followings are courted with samples and early information, and should disclose such favours. Online retailers add their own recommendations; Kotler and Keller cite one estimate that recommendation systems contribute 10 to 30 per cent of an online retailer's sales.

Identify, Differentiate, Interact, Customise.

blocks.title: Customer retention and loyalty
blocks.html:
Churn has common causes: poor service, unmet expectations, billing errors and complex processes. To manage it, a firm measures its retention rate, identifies why customers leave, compares the cost of keeping them with the profit they bring, and improves what it controls.

Customer base management (Kotler and Keller) aims to reduce churn, increase the length of relationships, raise each customer's value through cross-selling and up-selling, make low-profit customers more profitable or let them go, and give high-value customers disproportionate attention. Customers can be segmented by loyalty, profitability and engagement, and a marketing funnel (awareness, interest, purchase, loyalty) shows where they drop out.

Reducing defection. Adding customers while losing others is like pouring water into a leaking bucket. The firm should define and measure its retention rate, distinguish the causes of attrition and identify those it can manage, and compare a lost customer's lifetime value with the cost of reducing defection. The marketing funnel shows what share of the target market reaches each stage, from aware to loyal; the conversion rate between stages reveals bottlenecks, as when far fewer triers become repeat users. Growing each customer's value also means raising share of wallet.

Three kinds of activity improve loyalty and retention: interacting with customers and listening to them; loyalty programmes, both frequency programmes that reward customers who buy often and in quantity, and club membership programmes, open to all buyers or to an affinity group or a fee-paying few; and institutional ties, such as equipment or computer links that help customers manage orders, payroll and inventory.

Building loyalty. Leonard Berry and A. Parasuraman (1991) described three levels of relationship marketing, each binding the customer more tightly.

LevelHowExamples
Financial benefitsRewards that lower the customer's costDiscounts, cashback, frequency programmes
Social benefitsPersonal ties with staff and other customersExclusive events, communities, club memberships
Structural tiesLinks built into the customer's own systemsTechnology integration, customised solutions

Other loyalty builders: superior products and experiences, listening to the voice of the customer, easy complaint channels, and recognising employees who serve customers well.

Financial, social, structural: each binds more tightly.

blocks.title: The CRM value chain and process
blocks.html:
Francis Buttle's CRM value chain (2004) has five primary stages: customer portfolio analysis (which customers to serve), customer intimacy (knowing them), network development (with suppliers, partners and employees), value proposition development, and managing the customer lifecycle (acquisition, retention, development). They rest on four supporting conditions: leadership and culture, data and IT, people and processes. Shorter versions often leave out customer intimacy.

StepAim
1 Generate brand awarenessMake target customers know the brand
2 Acquire leadsDraw interested prospects into contact
3 Convert leads into customersTurn prospects into buyers
4 Provide quality customer supportKeep customers satisfied
5 Drive upsellingGrow each customer's value with higher-value or added products

In the process, marketing builds buyer personas, fictional profiles of ideal customers by demographics, interests, values and challenges, to target awareness campaigns; lead generation draws prospects into the sales funnel through sign-up forms, chat and content; lead scoring helps sales staff spot the prospects most likely to buy; support teams gather feedback after purchase; and upselling offers warranties or higher-featured products.

What CRM systems do: record leads and contacts and sort them into customers, lost customers, prospects, suppliers, partners and influencers; track every interaction centrally so all staff see the history; reveal prospects not yet sold to; and keep customer data even when staff move on. Their benefits are higher conversion rates, closer relationships, better business performance through cross-selling, up-selling and referrals, and higher employee productivity through automating tasks such as email, lead scoring and pipeline management. Cloud-based CRM adds flexibility and access from anywhere.

Awareness, leads, conversion, support, upselling.

text: Berry and Parasuraman's first two levels bind customers by rewards and by personal ties. The Kuṟaḷ says that one who is generous in giving and speaks kindly will be surrounded by kin, ring upon ring. It describes how a person keeps relatives close, not how a firm keeps customers.
pairings.quote: “One who gives and speaks kindly will be surrounded by kin, ring upon ring.” கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின் அடுக்கிய சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப் படும். Tirukkuṟaḷ 525

pairings.classic: the thread that leaves a knot
text: Rahim warns against snapping the thread of affection: once broken it does not join, and if it is joined a knot remains. Retention work makes the same point about customers: winning back one who left costs more than keeping them, and the relationship rarely returns to what it was. Rahim wrote of personal bonds, so this is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Rahim, do not snap the thread of love with a jerk. Once broken it will not join again, and if it does, a knot remains.” रहिमन धागा प्रेम का, मत तोड़ो चटकाय । टूटे से फिर ना मिले, मिले गाँठ परि जाय ॥ rahiman dhāgā prem kā, mat toṛo chaṭkāy; ṭūṭe se phir nā mile, mile gā̃ṭh pari jāy. Rahīm, dohā (Hindi)

chapters.title: Retail Marketing
chapters.scope: What retailers do, the kinds of store and non-store retailers, how retailers organise, and recent trends in Indian and world retail.

blocks.title: Retailing and store retailers
blocks.html:
Retailing is all the activities involved in selling goods or services directly to final consumers for their personal, non-business use. The retailer is the final link in the distribution channel: it connects manufacturers with consumers, creates satisfaction, and passes customer feedback back up the chain. Retail channels include physical stores, mail order, telephone, vending machines and online stores.

A retailer is any business whose sales come mainly from retailing; but any organisation selling to final consumers, whether manufacturer, wholesaler or retailer, is doing retailing, however the goods are sold (in person, by mail, phone, vending machine or online) and wherever (in a store, on the street or at home).

Kotler and Armstrong classify store retailers by the amount of service, the product line sold, relative prices, and how they are organised. Supermarkets are classified by product line.

Service levelFeature
Self-serviceCustomers serve themselves; lowest prices
Self-selectionCustomers shop on their own, with help available
Limited serviceMore help, credit and returns, and knowledgeable staff
Full serviceSalespeople help throughout; premium stores
TypeDescription
Specialty storeA narrow but deep product line, with expert advice
Department storeSeveral product lines, each run as a separate department
SupermarketA large, low-cost, low-margin, high-volume, self-service store for groceries and household products
Convenience storeA small store near homes, open long hours, selling a limited line of fast-moving goods
Drug store (pharmacy)Medicines and health products, sometimes with clinics
Discount storeStandard goods at lower prices, accepting lower margins for higher volume
Hard discounterA limited assortment at very low prices
Off-price retailerLeftover, surplus or irregular branded goods below regular prices, as in factory outlets
SuperstoreA very large store for routinely bought food and non-food items, with services; includes category killers, which carry a deep assortment in one line
Catalogue showroomA broad selection of discounted branded goods, ordered from a catalogue

By service, by product line, by price, by organisation.

blocks.title: Non-store and corporate retailing
blocks.html:
FormHow it works
Direct sellingPersonal selling at home or work, including multi-level marketing
Direct marketingMail, telemarketing, TV shopping and the internet
Automatic vendingUnmanned machines selling around the clock; convenience and impulse goods
Buying serviceServes a specific clientele, often employees of large organisations, who get discounts from selected retailers
FormDescription
Corporate chainTwo or more outlets under common ownership and control, with central buying and merchandising
Voluntary chainIndependent retailers organised by a wholesaler for group buying and common merchandising
Retailer cooperativeIndependent retailers who set up a central buying organisation and run joint promotions
Consumer cooperativeA retail firm owned by its customers, who contribute capital, vote on policy, elect managers and receive dividends; Mumbai's Apna Bazar is an example
Franchise organisationA contractual system in which franchisees run outlets under the franchisor's brand and system, for a fee
Merchandising conglomerateA corporation owning several diversified retail brands and formats

Corporate retail organisations gain economies of scale, greater buying power, wider brand recognition and better-trained staff than independent stores usually can. Lijjat Papad is often given as an example of a consumer cooperative; in fact it is a cooperative of the women who make its products, not one owned by its customers.

Private labels (also called reseller, store, house or distributor brands) are a retailer's own brands, as Marks & Spencer, Benetton and The Body Shop sell. They give the retailer more control over price and quality, higher margins and stronger customer loyalty.

Chain, voluntary chain, cooperative, franchise, conglomerate.

blocks.title: Trends in Indian and world retail
blocks.html:
TrendWhat is happening
Demographic changeDual-income and nuclear families with more discretionary spending
Convenience shoppingMalls and organised retail offering one-stop shopping
Online retailRapid growth of e-commerce as internet use spreads
TechnologyBarcode scanners, CCTV, digital signage and retail automation
Digital paymentsCards, UPI and digital wallets reducing cash use
ExpansionGrowth into Tier-II and Tier-III cities
Kirana modernisationNeighbourhood stores adding self-service, home delivery, credit and digital ordering
PartnershipsAlliances and joint ventures that share investment and risk
Government policyFDI rules: 100 per cent in single-brand retail through the automatic route since 2018; up to 51 per cent in multi-brand retail with government approval since 2012
Smarter consumersResearching products online before buying
TrendWhat is happening
New retail forms and combinationsBookshops with cafés, fuel stations with food stores, bank branches and services inside malls
Intertype competitionDiscount stores, catalogue showrooms and department stores all compete for the same buyers with the same merchandise
Store against non-store retailingDirect mail, TV, phones and the internet take business from stores, which answer with their own websites and more engaging in-store experiences
Giant retailersSuperior information systems, logistics and buying power let large chains offer good service and huge volumes at appealing prices
Investment in technologyBetter forecasts, inventory control, electronic ordering, and in-store screens
Global retailersRetailers with distinctive formats and strong positioning, such as IKEA and Apple, expand abroad
Shopper marketingKotler and Keller report that 70 to 80 per cent of purchase decisions are made in the store, so firms work to influence buyers at the point of purchase
Store design and entertainmentLayouts that draw people in, keep them longer and encourage impulse buying; food courts, cinemas, play areas and cafés

In India, buying behaviour is far from uniform across income groups; organised retail has made less impact on lower-income shoppers, and small independent retailers survive by offering personal service. Organised retail needs trained staff, and technology gives it cost and service advantages over unorganised players.

Organised, online, digital and reaching smaller towns.

pairings.modern: Trust at the point of sale
text: The Arthaśāstra appoints a superintendent of weights and measures to make and stamp the standard ones, and in Book 4 fines traders who cheat buyers with false weights and measures. A retailer's business still rests on that trust at the point of sale.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.19; traders at 4.2

chapters.title: International Marketing
chapters.scope: Why firms go abroad, how they choose and enter foreign markets, and the steps of the global marketing process.

blocks.title: Going international
blocks.html:
International marketing applies marketing principles across national borders to satisfy diverse customer needs. Global leaders such as Coca-Cola, Samsung, Honda and Sony draw on advantages in R&D, scale, global logistics, marketing expertise and finance. Supply chains are global too: Kotler and Keller's example is Otis Elevator, which drew door systems from France, gears from Spain, electronics from Germany and motors from Japan, with systems integration in the United States.

Why go internationalRisks
Higher market growthDifferent customer preferences
Economies of scaleCultural differences
Spreading risk across marketsRegulatory complexity
Competitive advantagePolitical and economic instability
Serving existing customers who have gone globalCurrency fluctuations
StageDescription
1No regular export activity: domestic operations only
2Exports through independent agents
3Export department and sales subsidiaries abroad
4Production and marketing facilities abroad

Commitment and risk rise from stage to stage. This stepwise pattern follows the Uppsala studies of Swedish firms (Jan Johanson and Finn Wiedersheim-Paul, 1975).

The global marketing process: identify and evaluate opportunities, decide the market entry strategy, develop the marketing programme, implement it, and monitor and control.

Domestic, agents, subsidiaries, production abroad.

blocks.title: Selecting foreign markets
blocks.html:
Firms weigh product suitability, geographic proximity, economic potential and political stability. Many prefer psychic proximity: countries with a similar language, culture and legal system, as US firms have often entered Canada, the UK and Australia first.

AspectWaterfallSprinkler
EntryCountry by country, in sequenceMany countries at once
Risk and investmentLower; learning from each marketHigher investment
AdvantageControlled expansion and learningFirst-mover advantage before rivals copy
ExamplesBMW, General ElectricMicrosoft's simultaneous worldwide launch of Windows

Emerging markets, notably the BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa), offer untapped demand, high growth and an expanding middle class. Winning there calls for affordable prices, adapted products and local marketing, as with Unilever's small, affordable sachets and Colgate-Palmolive's video vans touring rural India.

Similar markets first, or many at once.

blocks.title: Modes of entry
blocks.html:
Kotler and Keller arrange entry modes in order of increasing commitment, risk, control and profit potential.

ModeHow it worksInvestmentRiskControl
Indirect exportingSelling through independent intermediaries at homeLowLowLow
Direct exportingThe company handles its own exports, through its own export department, branches or agentsMediumMediumHigher
LicensingA foreign firm gets the right to use a process, trademark or patent for a royalty; also management contracts, contract manufacturing and franchising (as Marriott, Hyatt and McDonald's use)LowLowLow; the licensee may become a competitor
Joint venturePartnership with local firms sharing ownership, risk and profitMediumSharedShared
Direct investment (FDI)Building or buying production facilities abroadVery highHighFull

Joint ventures bring local expertise, shared resources and easier government approval, and have been common in China and India. FDI gives full control, lower production cost in some markets, a strong local image and better market access.

Export, license, joint venture, invest: more commitment, more control.

text: The Arthaśāstra's director of trade, for trade in a foreign land, is to compare the price and value of the goods to be exchanged, and to reckon the duties, road cess, escort charges, ferry dues and other costs before judging the profit; he should also seek the friendship of officials along the way. That is a foreign-market assessment of cost, price and access before entry.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 2.16

text: Market selection comes before entry. The Kuṟaḷ says to begin no undertaking and to despise no enemy until one has seen the place from which to act. It is military advice about ground, not about countries as markets.
pairings.quote: “Begin no undertaking and scorn no foe until you have found the place to act from.” தொடங்கற்க எவ்வினையும் எள்ளற்க முற்றும் இடங்கண்ட பின்அல் லது. Tirukkuṟaḷ 491

chapters.title: Emerging Trends in Marketing
chapters.scope: Social and green marketing, online, digital and direct marketing, rural marketing, and unconventional tactics such as guerrilla and roadblock marketing.

blocks.title: Social marketing and green marketing
blocks.html:
Social marketing applies commercial marketing techniques to influence behaviour that benefits individuals and society. Philip Kotler and Gerald Zaltman introduced the idea in 1971. Its key components are a target audience, a desired behaviour change, exchange theory (the change must offer benefits that outweigh its perceived costs) and a marketing mix. India's pulse polio and Swachh Bharat campaigns are examples.

ObjectivesBehaviour change, community development, public participation, social welfare
StrategiesMedia and social media campaigns, community engagement, partnerships with NGOs and government
ChallengesCultural sensitivity; measuring long-term impact

Green marketing markets environmentally sustainable products and practices: eco-friendly products, sustainable processes, eco-labelling and green advertising. Its aims are to promote eco-friendly consumption and build a responsible brand image; its tools include transparency, CSR initiatives and attention to the whole product life cycle. Its main risk is greenwashing: false or exaggerated environmental claims, which breed consumer scepticism. Green products may also cost more to make.

Sell behaviour change for society; sell sustainability honestly.

blocks.title: Green marketing in practice
blocks.html:
Green marketing promotes products on the strength of their environmental advantages, through product changes, cleaner processes, sustainable packaging and green advertising, so as to reduce the harm a product does in its making, use and disposal. A green product allows economic development while conserving resources for future generations: it neither pollutes the earth nor depletes natural resources, and it can be recycled or conserved. Companies look at three things: the raw materials, the product itself, and its packaging.

Objectives: to meet corporate social responsibility, reduce costs, show how environment-friendly the offering is, communicate the brand message, and adopt sustainable, socially accountable practices. Benefits for the business: competitive advantage as consumers grow more aware, lower operating costs (natural light, water conservation, recycling), and a positive brand image that attracts talent and investors.

PGreen approach
ProductDesigned to use fewer resources, cause no pollution and be reusable or recyclable
PriceBuyers pay a premium only when they see added value, such as better performance, design or health benefits
PromotionAdvertising that links the product to the environment, promotes a green lifestyle, or presents a green corporate image
PlaceMaking green products available where and how buyers can get them, which strongly affects who buys

Practices: recycled and renewable materials, green energy (solar, wind, geothermal), less or eco-friendly packaging, avoiding toxic materials, and reusable, recyclable products. Strategies: green design, green positioning, green pricing, and green disposal systems for what the product leaves behind.

PrincipleMeaning
Consumer-oriented marketingSee marketing activities from the consumer's point of view
Customer-value marketingPut resources into building real customer value
Innovative marketingKeep seeking real improvements in products and marketing
Sense-of-mission marketingDefine the mission in broad social terms rather than narrow product terms
Societal marketingWeigh consumers' wants, the company's needs, consumers' long-term interests and society's interests

These are often presented as principles of green marketing; they are Kotler and Armstrong's principles of sustainable marketing, which green marketing applies. Greenwashing, claiming green habits a firm does not practise, misleads buyers and erodes trust.

Green product, price, place and promotion; green design, positioning, pricing and disposal.

blocks.title: Online and direct marketing
blocks.html:
Online (digital) marketing uses digital platforms for targeted, measurable and scalable customer engagement, aiming at brand awareness, website traffic, conversion and engagement.

ComponentPurpose
Search engine optimisation (SEO)Improve search rankings
Content marketingBlogs, videos and e-books that attract and inform
Social media marketingCustomer engagement
Email marketingPersonalised communication
Pay-per-click (PPC) advertisingPaid clicks and traffic

Strategies include inbound marketing (drawing customers with useful content), affiliate marketing and influencer marketing. In performance marketing advertisers pay only when a measurable action, such as a click, lead or sale, occurs. Challenges include data privacy (in India, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023), ad blockers and changing algorithms.

Direct marketing is one-to-one communication designed to get an immediate, measurable response: direct mail, telemarketing, email, catalogues and direct-response advertising. It relies on personalisation, a strong call to action, and tracking response and return on investment; its challenges are intrusiveness, managing the customer database and complying with regulations.

Targeted, measurable and paid for by results.

blocks.title: Digital marketing
blocks.html:
TermScope
Internet marketingUsing the internet to win customers, mainly through a website, search engine optimisation and pay-per-click ads, and converting that traffic into sales
E-marketingInternet marketing plus relationship building: email, online reviews, referral programmes, social media and CRM
Digital marketingThe widest term: all marketing through digital interfaces, online or not, including mobile apps and push notifications, in-app ads, electronic billboards and digital databases

Unlike traditional marketing, which is largely one-way, digital marketing allows two-way communication, and it reaches people where they spend more and more of their time: on screens.

MethodWhat it is
Search engine marketing (SEM)Paid advertising to raise visibility in search results, often used with SEO
Affiliate marketingPerformance-based revenue sharing, paying affiliates per sale made through their referral
Native advertisingPaid content that blends into the medium around it, such as sponsored articles; it should be clearly labelled ‘sponsored’ or ‘promoted’
Marketing automationSoftware that schedules social media posts, runs lead-nurturing email workflows and tracks campaigns

Benefits: global reach, a low cost of entry, measurable return on investment, precise targeting, the flexibility to change course quickly, an immediate connection with buyers who research online, relationship building through social media, and easy conversion, since a buyer can act at once.

Budgets scale with the firm: basic (websites, blogs and social media for start-ups), intermediate (adding SEO, SEM, PPC and email for medium firms) and advanced (comprehensive, often global, strategies for large firms). Building a strategy: identify marketing goals, settle the digital sales process, define target customers and buyer personas, choose channels, set clear benchmarks, and adjust as results come in.

Goals, sales process, personas, channels, benchmarks, adjustment.

blocks.title: Rural marketing
blocks.html:
Rural marketing designs strategies for rural consumers: penetrating rural markets, meeting local needs and helping raise living standards. It needs efficient distribution, affordable prices (small packs and sachets), products adapted to rural conditions, and promotion in local languages.

Indian practitioners often frame rural marketing in four As: availability, affordability, acceptability and awareness. Strategies use local opinion leaders, weekly markets (haats), agriculture-linked marketing, folk media and street campaigns. Challenges are logistics, poor infrastructure and cultural and linguistic diversity.

Available, affordable, acceptable, known.

blocks.title: Guerrilla and roadblock marketing
blocks.html:
AspectGuerrilla marketingRoadblock marketing
IdeaCreative, unconventional, low-cost tactics that surprise people and create buzz (Jay Conrad Levinson, Guerrilla Marketing, 1984)Advertising on many channels at the same time, so the audience meets the message wherever it turns
ObjectivesAttention, viral publicity, brand recallMaximum reach, high recall, strong visibility
TacticsStreet marketing, viral campaigns, experiential marketingPrime-time TV roadblocks, digital and radio roadblocks, coordinated media buying
ChallengesLegal permissions, ethical concerns, hard-to-measure returnsHigh cost, keeping the message consistent, ad fatigue

Guerrilla surprises cheaply; roadblock saturates expensively.

pairings.classic: what is taken, may it grow back
text: Green marketing asks that consumption leave the earth able to renew itself. The Atharvaveda's hymn to the Earth prays that what is dug from her may quickly grow again, and that her vitals and heart not be wounded. It is a prayer, not a policy, but it states the idea of renewal plainly.
pairings.quote: यत्ते भूमे विखनामि क्षिप्रं तदपि रोहतु । yat te bhūme vikhanāmi kṣipraṃ tad api rohatu. “What I dig from you, O Earth, may that quickly grow again.” Atharvaveda 12.1.35

text: Greenwashing wins sales with false claims. The Kuṟaḷ says that wealth gained by deceit and kept is like water poured into an unbaked clay pot: it will not hold. It speaks of deceit in general, not of environmental claims.
pairings.quote: “Guarding wealth gained by deceit is like keeping water in a pot of unbaked clay.” சலத்தால் பொருள்செய்தே மார்த்தல் பசுமண் கலத்துள்நீர் பெய்திரீஇ யற்று. Tirukkuṟaḷ 660

text: Rural marketing starts from the size and importance of the farm economy. The Kuṟaḷ says that however the world turns, it follows the plough, and so farming, though hard, is foremost. It praises agriculture; it does not speak of markets.
pairings.quote: “However it wanders, the world follows the plough; so farming, though toilsome, is foremost.” சுழன்றும்ஏர்ப் பின்னது உலகம் அதனால் உழந்தும் உழவே தலை. Tirukkuṟaḷ 1031
